questions.modelOutline: Open with the principle: the model is not a security boundary, so the agent must operate with the user's entitlements enforced at retrieval, before anything reaches the context window. Mechanism: identity from a verified JWT; a mandatory metadata filter (matter, group, privileged flag) on every Knowledge Base Retrieve call built by your code, like a terms filter on every Elasticsearch query; optionally ACL-aware connectors or OpenSearch document-level security as a second layer. Defence in depth: re-check returned document ids against authz and fail closed, alert on violations. Ethical walls exclude the matter entirely, not just the content. Prove it with cross-boundary tests in CI, plain and adversarial, asserting zero chunks and no leaked content. Close with the ERP parallel (RBAC in the API, not the UI) and the trade-off: ingestion metadata becomes a security surface.
rubric: States that the model/context window is not a security boundary
Enforcement at retrieval with a filter derived from verified identity, built by application code
Names a concrete AWS mechanism (KB metadata filtering, ACL connector, OpenSearch DLS)
Post-retrieval re-check of document ids, fail closed, alert
Ethical wall: exclude the matter entirely, including existence
Cross-boundary tests with adversarial phrasing as a CI gate
Mentions a trade-off or operational cost (ingestion metadata discipline)

questions.prompt: How do you handle prompt injection in retrieved documents?
questions.modelOutline: Define direct versus indirect injection and say why eDiscovery is worst case: the documents come from the opposing party. State the premise that detection is imperfect, so design so a successful injection is harmless. Layers: read-only tools by default and every write-capable tool behind human approval with a plain-language summary; least-privilege IAM per tool plus step and token budgets to bound blast radius; output handling so model output never reaches SQL, shell or HTML unparameterised (OWASP LLM05); Guardrails prompt-attack and PII filters, ApplyGuardrail on retrieved chunks, delimiters marking content as data, all as probabilistic detection. Use OWASP vocabulary: LLM01, LLM06 Excessive Agency. Test with seeded injected documents asserting no unapproved write. Close with the SQL injection analogy and its limit: there is no parameterised query for language.
rubric: Distinguishes direct from indirect injection; retrieved content and tool outputs are untrusted
Premise: cannot reliably detect, so make a successful injection harmless
Write-capable tools behind human approval with a readable summary
Per-tool least privilege and step/token budgets
Output handling: no unparameterised sinks (LLM05)
Guardrails/ApplyGuardrail and delimiting framed as probabilistic, not sufficient
Uses OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 vocabulary correctly (LLM01, LLM06)
Seeded injection tests in the eval suite

questions.prompt: A senior partner at the law firm, who is not technical, asks why the review agent needs a human to approve before it tags documents as privileged. Explain your decision to her.
questions.modelOutline: Drop the jargon. Lead with her risk: a document wrongly marked not-privileged and produced to the other side cannot be un-produced, and privilege waiver is her problem, not a software bug. Use one analogy from her world: the agent is a brilliant first-year associate who has read everything and never sleeps, but a partner still signs the privilege log. Then the design in one sentence: the agent proposes, a reviewer confirms in batches with a one-line reason, and every decision is recorded so the firm can show the court how privilege was determined. Give the cost honestly: a few seconds per document, and say what you did to minimise it (bulk approval, confidence sorting). Offer the lever: as the audit shows the agent's accuracy on her matter types, the threshold for auto-approval can be negotiated, with her, not by engineers. End by asking what she would need to see to be comfortable.
rubric: No unexplained jargon; speaks in the partner's terms of risk and consequence
Names the irreversible consequence (production, privilege waiver) up front
Uses one concrete analogy from legal practice
States the design in one plain sentence: propose, confirm, record
Honest about the cost and what was done to reduce it
Offers a path to loosen the control based on measured accuracy, decided by the partner
Ends with a question or invitation rather than a lecture

questions.prompt: The agent just showed a paralegal a summary of a privileged memo from a matter she is walled off from. Walk me through the next 72 hours.
questions.modelOutline: Hour zero: contain. Disable the affected path or the agent for that firm, revoke nothing that destroys evidence. Preserve: the audit record for the request (prompt, chunk ids, modelId, answer), invocation logs, and put a legal hold on them. Reconstruct from the trail: was it a retrieval filter failure, missing metadata on ingestion, a connector ACL lag, or an injection? Scope: query the audit store for every request that touched that matter's chunks from users outside it. Notify: the firm's general counsel and DPO immediately, because they own the Article 33 72-hour clock and any professional-conduct disclosure; give them facts, not speculation. Fix: the root cause, then a cross-boundary regression test that would have caught it, run in CI. Within 72 hours: written incident report with timeline, scope, cause, fix and the control added. Close: what you change in the process, for example boundary tests as a release gate.
rubric: Immediate containment without destroying evidence
Preservation of the audit trail and logs, legal hold applied
Root-cause reconstruction from the per-request trace (chunk ids, filter, modelId)
Scoping the blast radius by querying the audit store for similar requests
Prompt notification of the firm's counsel/DPO with the 72-hour GDPR clock in mind
Fix plus a regression test added as a CI gate
Written incident report with timeline, scope, cause, fix
A process change, not just a code change
